## Claude synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Ambali, Jung, and Sorensen link the 2015 New York State Building Condition Survey — engineer- or architect-led inspections that state law requires for every occupied public school building — to enrollment and district-finance data for roughly 2,350 traditional public schools outside New York City, and document large, item-specific racial gaps in the realized physical condition of schools. That descriptive core is the paper's contribution and it is trustworthy: relative to schools more than 80% White, schools more than 50% non-White are 25.9 percentage points less likely to have a satisfactory ventilation system, 20.0 points less likely to have satisfactory humidity, 17.3 points less likely to have a good appearance rating, 14.6 points less likely to be rated clean, 19.4 points less likely to have athletic fields, 11.5 points less likely to have a health office, and 7.1 points more likely to have mold (Table 1), and the student-weighted exposure analysis shows that Hispanic students (−0.32 SD on the overall index) and Black students (−0.19 SD) bear these gaps while Asian, multiracial, American Indian/Alaska Native, and White students attend above-average buildings (Figure 2). These numbers are internally consistent — Figure 1 reproduces the pooled Table 1 means, the index rows are exact averages of their items, and the text quotes the tables accurately with one swap — and they are large enough to survive the district-level clustering the paper does not do. The field should be far more careful with the second half of the paper, which is what the abstract leads with and what policy audiences will quote. The Kitagawa-Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition (Table 2, Figure 3) is arithmetically faithful — property taxes' 30%, donations' 7%, and state building aid's −17% recompute exactly as E + C + I for each covariate over the 0.0830 gap — but Table 2 omits the constant term, and the listed covariate coefficient rows sum to about −0.010 against a reported coefficients component of 0.0603, so roughly 0.070 (84% of the overall gap; more than the entire gap for the aesthetics and environmental indices) sits in an unreported intercept difference that neither the table nor Figure 3 shows. The paper's reading of the large coefficients component as evidence that funding channels "have different associations ... in ways that exacerbate inequality" (p. 8) therefore attributes to the covariates a quantity that is almost entirely the unexplained residual. The per-covariate "percent explained" bars also mix an invariant endowment piece with coefficient and interaction pieces that depend on where each variable's zero sits — and the interaction-to-coefficient ratios in Table 2 (−2.17 for property taxes in all four columns) imply the continuous finance variables were centered in a way the paper never reports. On the invariant endowment piece alone, property-tax differences account for 51% of the gap under the paper's non-White-coefficient reference and 12% under the White-coefficient reference; state aid for −13% and −31%; donations for a non-significant 2%. Add robust rather than district-clustered standard errors on district-level finance regressors, causal language ("successfully helping to equalize," p. 11; "helps reduce these disparities," abstract) that contradicts the authors' own p. 5 caveat, the mechanical link between reimbursement-style building aid and recent construction, two Table 1 significance markers the reported means and cell sizes cannot produce, and an analytic sample that is 2,352 in the text, 2,371 in Table 1, and 1,440 rather than 1,459 in Table 2, and the right posture is: cite the paper for the existence, size, and item profile of inspection-based racial gaps in school facilities in New York outside NYC as of 2015, and for the student-weighted incidence on Hispanic and Black students; treat the finance decomposition as a directional association (local property-tax capacity lines up with the gap, state building aid lines up against it) rather than as the specific percentages or the policy verdicts the abstract offers.

> **Correction (2026-09-26).** The arithmetic here is right; the charge that the paper misreads it is withdrawn. Table 2 prints no constant row, and the overall-index coefficient rows do sum to −0.0095 against the reported 0.0603, so about 0.070 (84% of the 0.0830 gap) sits in the unprinted Kitagawa–Oaxaca–Blinder intercept. But the 30% recomputes exactly ((0.0425 + 0.0151 − 0.0328)/0.0830 = 29.9%), every Figure 3 bar recomputes from Table 2, and the paper never claims that the listed covariates account for the whole gap. This is a reporting omission (no constant row, so a reader cannot check the total) rather than a text–table discrepancy, and it was removed from the audit's list of errors after a blind second reading. The advice to describe property taxes as the largest identified contributor to a gap the model mostly does not explain remains sound; the description of the paper's reading as an error does not. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed by recomputation from the rendered table.

#### Key Strengths

- The outcome is realized building condition from a statutory, professionally conducted inspection census — 2,473 of 2,875 traditional public schools outside NYC (86%), the last full-census wave before the BCS moved to annual samples of 500–560 schools — not dollars spent. Moving from capital outlay (Brunner et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2022) to the ventilation, humidity, mold, and facility access students actually experience is the paper's clearest conceptual contribution and fills a genuine gap.
- The descriptive exhibits are item-level, large, and internally consistent. Twenty-four items across three domains are reported by school racial composition with means and tests (Table 1); the index rows are exact averages of their items; Figure 1 matches the pooled Table 1 means to two decimals on every item; and the gaps on the dimensions the mechanism literature cares most about (ventilation −25.9 pp, humidity −20.0 pp, mold +7.1 pp, health office −11.5 pp, all p < .01) are too large for clustering or rater effects to erase.
- The student-weighted exposure analysis (Figure 2) unbundles the coarse ">50% non-White" category and shows that the disadvantage falls specifically on Hispanic (−0.32 SD overall) and Black (−0.19 SD) students, while Asian (+0.05), multiracial (+0.10), AIAN (+0.15), and White (+0.21) students attend above-average buildings. All 24 cell values quoted in the text match the rendered figure. This is the paper's most distinctive and citable exhibit.
- The decomposition is fully reported and fully recomputable: the threefold equations are written out with the non-White coefficients as reference (p. 4); Table 2 gives all twelve covariates' endowment, coefficient, and interaction terms with SEs for all four indices; E + C + I equals the gap in every column; and every bar in Figure 3 (30% property taxes, 7% donations, −17% state aid, and the smaller ones) recomputes exactly from Table 2.
- The authors state the limits plainly where it counts: the decomposition "remains descriptive and could contain bias due to omitted variables or reverse causality" and "does not establish causal relationships" (p. 5); the data are one cross-section; the items may be subjective (p. 12). The literature review's typology of the capital-spending evidence (null / delayed / strong) is fair and does not cherry-pick, and citation integrity is clean (all 52 references cited; no dangling in-text citations).

#### Key Concerns

- Most of the decomposed gap is in an unreported intercept, and the text reads it as a covariate result. Table 2's detailed endowment and interaction rows sum to their totals, but the coefficient rows sum to about −0.0095 for the overall index against a reported coefficients component of 0.0603; the implied constant is about 0.070 (84% of the 0.0830 gap), about 0.093 for aesthetics (105% of that gap), 0.091 for environment (151%), and 0.026 for health/recreation. Figure 3 shows no bar for it, so all twelve covariate bars together net to roughly 16% of the overall gap while the property-tax bar alone reads 30%. The p. 8 sentence attributing the large coefficients component to funding channels having "different associations ... in ways that exacerbate inequality" is not what the listed rows show; across the covariates, the coefficient differences net to zero or slightly negative.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The arithmetic here is right; the charge that the paper misreads it is withdrawn. Table 2 prints no constant row, and the overall-index coefficient rows do sum to −0.0095 against the reported 0.0603, so about 0.070 (84% of the 0.0830 gap) sits in the unprinted Kitagawa–Oaxaca–Blinder intercept. But the 30% recomputes exactly ((0.0425 + 0.0151 − 0.0328)/0.0830 = 29.9%), every Figure 3 bar recomputes from Table 2, and the paper never claims that the listed covariates account for the whole gap. This is a reporting omission (no constant row, so a reader cannot check the total) rather than a text–table discrepancy, and it was removed from the audit's list of errors after a blind second reading. The advice to describe property taxes as the largest identified contributor to a gap the model mostly does not explain remains sound; the description of the paper's reading as an error does not. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed by recomputation from the rendered table.

- The per-covariate percentages depend on unreported normalization choices. Under the p. 4 equations, I_k/C_k = (X̄_W − X̄_NW)/X̄_NW, which is constant across outcome columns for each covariate (it is: −2.17 for property taxes, about −1.30 for state aid, −1.44 federal aid, −1.24 bonds, −2.0 enrollment) and implies opposite-signed group means for every continuous variable — impossible for raw per-pupil dollars or enrollment, so those variables were centered or standardized without disclosure, while the locale and school-level dummies (same-sign ratios) were not. Coefficient and interaction contributions are not invariant to such shifts (Oaxaca & Ransom, 1999; Jann, 2008), reference categories for the dummies are never stated, and the "pp = thousands of dollars per pupil" note is at best incomplete. The invariant endowment shares tell a more modest story: property taxes 51% (or 12% with White coefficients as reference), state aid −13% (−31%), donations 2% and not significant.
- Causal wording outruns the descriptive design, especially for state building aid and donations. The abstract says aid "helps reduce these disparities," the introduction that it "meaningfully narrows infrastructure gaps," and the Results that the progressive formula "is successfully helping to equalize gaps" (p. 11), against the authors' own p. 5 caveat. New York building aid reimburses approved capital projects, so districts that recently built receive more aid per pupil and have better-rated buildings; the association is what one would see even if the formula equalized nothing, and the state-aid contribution flips sign (+0.0057) for the health/recreation index. The donations claim ("contribute meaningfully," p. 12) rests entirely on the location-dependent coefficient term (0.0056); the endowment (0.0020, SE 0.0012) is not significant and E + I ≈ 0 in every column, implying β_W ≈ 0.
- Inference ignores the district structure, and two Table 1 stars cannot be right. Finance covariates are district-level comptroller data assigned to every school in a district, and each district hires its own inspection firm (so rater standards are district-level too), yet Table 2 reports robust, unclustered SEs and Table 1 uses simple two-group t-tests; the number of districts is never reported. Separately, swimming pool (0.152 vs 0.119, n = 940/519) is marked ** and the text repeats p < .01, but a two-proportion test gives t ≈ 1.8 (p ≈ .07); stadium condition (0.386 vs 0.162) is marked * but gives t ≈ 9.9. The other 22 rows reproduce. The cluster unit for the Figure 2 bootstrap is also unstated.
- The prose and exhibits disagree in several places a reader could be caught by, and nothing can be verified outside the article. Page 5 says "85% have good quality lighting, and 75% have a good appearance rating" — Figure 1a and the pooled Table 1 means show the reverse (appearance 0.85, lighting 0.75). The abstract lists gymnasiums among "significantly" reduced-access facilities (the gap is −0.025 at p < .1). The introduction describes the comparison group as "predominantly Black and Hispanic" when it is >50% non-White of any group. The analytic sample is 2,352 (text) but 2,371 (Table 1), and Table 2's N of 1,440 is 19 short of the 940 + 519 it compares; neither is explained. The "condition satisfactory" items are unconditional shares, so the athletic-field and stadium "condition" gaps largely restate presence gaps (conditional on having the facility, the satisfactory share is 0.889 W vs 0.913 NW for fields, 0.902 vs 0.895 for stadiums). There is no data-availability statement, no code, no software version, no access pathway for the NYSED-provided BCS file, and the poverty/locale comparisons, Figure 2 significance tests, Model 1–3 sensitivity, and latent-factor check live only in an online supplement not bundled with the PDF.

#### What to Rely On

- Large racial gaps in inspected building conditions exist in New York outside NYC as of 2015, on the dimensions that matter most for health and learning: relative to mostly-White schools, mostly-non-White schools are 25.9 pp less likely to have a satisfactory ventilation system, 20.0 pp less likely to have satisfactory humidity, 7.1 pp more likely to have mold, 17.3 pp less likely to have a good appearance rating, 14.6 pp less likely to be rated clean, and 8.1 pp less likely to be rated satisfactory overall (Table 1, all p < .01). Quote these from Table 1, not from the introduction's rounded versions.
- Access gaps in health and recreational facilities: mostly-non-White schools are 19.4 pp less likely to have athletic fields, 24.7 pp less likely to have an external stadium, and 11.5 pp less likely to have a health office in the building (Table 1, p < .01). Treat these as gaps in having the facility, not in its upkeep.
- The incidence falls on Hispanic and Black students specifically. Student-weighted, Hispanic students attend schools 0.32 SD below the mean on the overall index (−0.25 aesthetics, −0.24 environment, −0.16 recreation/health) and Black students 0.19 SD below (−0.16, −0.03, −0.19); Asian, multiracial, AIAN, and White students are at +0.05 to +0.21 (Figure 2). Note the SD unit is the student-weighted cross-school SD of each index, standardized separately, so do not compare magnitudes across columns.
- The overall condition of the stock: 84% of schools rated satisfactory overall, only 49% with central HVAC, 67% with satisfactory ventilation, 62% with satisfactory humidity, 92% mold-free, 68% with a playground, 32% with an external stadium, 13% with a pool, 90% with a health office (Figure 1; all verified against pooled Table 1 means).
- A directional finance association that holds across all four indices and under either reference group: differences in per-pupil local property-tax revenue are positively and significantly associated with the White/non-White gap (endowment terms 0.0425, 0.0583, 0.0254, 0.0437, all p < .01), and differences in state building aid are negatively associated with it for three of four indices (endowments −0.0107, −0.0257, −0.0100; the health/recreation term is +0.0036, n.s.). The paper reports that the property-tax share attenuates to roughly 20% once taxable property values and other community covariates enter (Model 3), consistent with property-tax revenue proxying local fiscal capacity — but that check is appendix-only.
- The paper's own framing of what it is: descriptive, cross-sectional, non-causal (pp. 5, 12).

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "Local property taxes are the largest contributor to racial gaps" / "explain 30%" / "nearly one-third" — the 30% is E + C + I for one covariate over a gap of which about 84% sits in an unreported constant; the twelve covariates together net to about 16%. The invariant endowment share is 51% under the paper's reference group and 12% under the other. Say "largest identified contributor to a gap the model mostly does not explain," and give a range rather than a point.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The arithmetic here is right; the charge that the paper misreads it is withdrawn. Table 2 prints no constant row, and the overall-index coefficient rows do sum to −0.0095 against the reported 0.0603, so about 0.070 (84% of the 0.0830 gap) sits in the unprinted Kitagawa–Oaxaca–Blinder intercept. But the 30% recomputes exactly ((0.0425 + 0.0151 − 0.0328)/0.0830 = 29.9%), every Figure 3 bar recomputes from Table 2, and the paper never claims that the listed covariates account for the whole gap. This is a reporting omission (no constant row, so a reader cannot check the total) rather than a text–table discrepancy, and it was removed from the audit's list of errors after a blind second reading. The advice to describe property taxes as the largest identified contributor to a gap the model mostly does not explain remains sound; the description of the paper's reading as an error does not. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed by recomputation from the rendered table.

- "State building aid helps reduce these disparities" / "is successfully helping to equalize gaps" — a counterfactual claim from a descriptive decomposition; only the endowment piece (−0.0107, p < .05) is significant, the −17% combines it with two non-significant terms, the sign flips for the health/recreation index, and reimbursement-style aid mechanically tracks recent construction. Read as: districts serving more students of color receive more building aid per pupil, and aid is positively associated with conditions.
- "Donations contribute meaningfully to the observed racial gaps" — the 7% comes entirely from the location-dependent coefficient term; the endowment (0.0020) is not significant and E + I ≈ 0, so the "White communities use wealth to donate" story is not supported by the invariant components.
- The p. 8 interpretation of the coefficients component as covariates having "different associations ... in ways that exacerbate inequality" — the covariate coefficient rows sum to −0.0095 (overall), −0.0047 (aesthetics), −0.0428 (environment); the positive total is the intercept. The same paragraph's "for most indices" understates: C > E in all four.
- Any Table 2 or Figure 3 percentage as a stable number — the continuous covariates appear centered without disclosure, omitted categories are unstated, and no `oaxaca` normalization options are reported; C and I terms move with those choices.
- Every significance star on a marginal item — SEs are robust, not district-clustered, on district-level regressors and district-run inspections; the number of districts is unreported. Treat vermin (+), heating (+), gymnasium (+), cooling satisfactory (*), and playground condition (*) as unresolved, and note that swimming pool (**) and stadium condition (*) carry stars the reported means and Ns cannot produce.
- "Athletic fields and external stadiums are also in worse condition" (pp. 2, 7) — the condition items are unconditional, and conditional on presence the satisfactory shares are equal or higher in mostly-non-White schools; these are presence gaps. The health/recreation index (the largest gap, 0.100) also counts presence twice for these items and weights stadiums and pools — amenities — equally with health offices.
- The p. 5 sentence "85% have good quality lighting, and 75% have a good appearance rating" — reversed; use Figure 1a (appearance 85%, lighting 75%). The introduction's "25 percentage points" for ventilation is 25.9 in Table 1. The abstract's "gymnasiums" is a −2.5 pp gap at p < .1.
- "Schools serving predominantly Black and Hispanic students" (p. 2) — the comparison group is >50% non-White of any group, pooling predominantly Asian suburban schools with high-poverty urban Black and Hispanic schools that Figure 2 shows have very different conditions; use Figure 2 for group-specific statements.
- "New York State" — New York City is excluded (note 2), the title and abstract do not say so, and NYC enrolls a large share of the state's Black and Hispanic students; the data are a single 2015 cross-section, and no comparable statewide census has been collected since.
- The Figure 2 significance statements (including "0.01 SD (p < .005)" and "0.00 SD (p < .05)") — tests against the most advantaged group for each index (which changes by index: AIAN for recreation and environment), from an unspecified cluster bootstrap, with results only in Appendix Table A7.
- The poverty-tier and locale comparisons (p. 8), the Model 1–3 sensitivity check ("roughly 30% to roughly 20%," p. 11), the latent-factor robustness (note 11), the representativeness claim for the 86% sample (note 4), and the index SDs of "0.14 to 0.17" (p. 8) — all rest on the online supplement or on nothing citable in the main text.
- The novelty claim "first comprehensive analysis ... using large-scale building inspection data" — defensible only through its qualifiers. GAO (1995) and NCES (2000) broke facility conditions out by minority enrollment (survey-based), Simons et al. (2010) and Sorensen et al. (2024) already used the New York BCS, and Brunner et al. (2023) is the primary antecedent for the property-wealth mechanism. Cite this paper for inspection-based, student-weighted, item-level gaps in one state, not for discovering that facilities differ by race or that local wealth drives them.
- Several literature characterizations worth checking before repeating: Duncombe & Wang (2009) cited as an outcomes study (it is a descriptive survey of state capital-funding programs); Baron, Hyman & Vasquez (2026) cited for capital-spending heterogeneity (its subject is operating funding and adult crime); Park et al. (2020) cited only for heat effects, without noting that it documents racial disparities in school air conditioning — the opposite of this paper's +3.6 pp cooling result, which the paper attributes to locale using appendix tables only.

## Codex synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful With Caveats

This paper provides useful inspection-based evidence of racial disparities in school facilities among traditional public schools outside New York City, using the 2015 Building Condition Survey (pp. 3–4, Data). Its strongest contribution is documenting specific differences in realized conditions: predominantly non-White schools have poorer ventilation, humidity, cleanliness, and health-office availability, while student-weighted comparisons show less favorable average conditions for Black and Hispanic students and distinct patterns for other groups (p. 6, Table 1; p. 7, Figure 2). My judgment is that these descriptive findings warrant selective citation despite weaknesses in exposition and reproducibility. The fiscal decomposition offers exploratory associations, not evidence that property-tax reliance causes the gaps or that state aid reduces them. Its headline shares are arithmetically reproducible, but incomplete component reporting, unclear dependence-adjusted inference, and unreconciled sample counts limit their explanatory weight (pp. 9–10, Table 2; p. 11, Figure 3). The study is a useful empirical extension of infrastructure-equity research, not a demonstrated policy evaluation or an estimate of student health or achievement effects.

#### Key Strengths

- Direct measures of realized conditions add information beyond capital expenditures: professionally supported inspections distinguish environmental conditions, aesthetics, and health/recreational facilities (pp. 3–4, Data). In my judgment, this linkage to demographics and finances is the paper's principal scholarly contribution.
- Substantively large item-level disparities support the descriptive conclusion independently of the composite: satisfactory ventilation is reported for 0.768 of mostly White schools versus 0.509 of mostly non-White schools, and health offices for 0.930 versus 0.815 (p. 6, Table 1). These are published descriptive estimates, not independently replicated population parameters.
- Separate school-composition and student-enrollment-weighted analyses clarify whose environments are being compared; the exhibits also reveal exceptions, including more favorable satisfactory-cooling and playground-condition proportions in predominantly non-White schools (p. 6, Table 1; p. 7, Figure 2).
- The literature discussion acknowledges heterogeneous findings on capital investments, and the methods explicitly explain the decomposition and its noncausal limits (pp. 2–5). This supports a useful descriptive reading even where the policy summaries exceed those limits.

#### Key Concerns

- Policy language exceeds identification: the methods state, “However, it does not establish causal relationships” (p. 5), but the results assert that the gap “would be larger in the absence of state building aid” (p. 10). My methodological judgment is that cross-sectional associations cannot identify this counterfactual, particularly when aid may respond to need.
- The decomposition is incompletely itemized. Table 2 reports “Coefficients” of “0.0603**,” but the displayed entries from “Middle school” through “Donations (pp)” sum to −0.0095, leaving 0.0698 unitemized (my calculation, pp. 9–10, Table 2). No constant row appears. An omitted intercept contribution is plausible, not verified; Figure 3 therefore cannot be treated as a complete substantive explanation of the gap (p. 11).
- Sample construction and replication remain underdocumented. Data reports “2,352 unique schools with full coverage of variables” (p. 4), whereas Table 1 lists “940,” “912,” and “519” schools, totaling 2,371; its extreme groups total 1,459, whereas Table 2 reports “Observations” of “1,440” (my sums, p. 6, Table 1; p. 10, Table 2). Different analysis samples could explain this, but the transitions, linkage rules, and missing-item coding are not established. The supplied article identifies no replication-code deposit, and referenced online appendices are unavailable here.
- Inferential precision is less secure than the descriptive pattern. Table 2 specifies “Robust standard errors in parentheses” without identifying district clustering (p. 10); the exposure bootstrap does not specify its resampling unit (p. 4). Figure 3 gives no uncertainty for combined contributions (p. 11). This is incomplete documentation, not proof that clustering was omitted.
- Summary prose and composite interpretations need qualification. The text says “Eighty-five percent have good quality lighting, and 75% have a good appearance rating,” whereas Figure 1a labels “Appearance good” as 0.85 and “Lighting quality good” as 0.75 (p. 5). More fundamentally, averaging amenity presence and condition ratings does not establish a common health or educational impact, and local ratings and unclear absent-facility coding constrain interpretation (pp. 3–4, 12).

#### What to Rely On

- Inspection-based descriptive disparities in the covered historical school population: mostly non-White schools have worse reported conditions on several consequential items, with exceptions rather than uniform disadvantage across facilities (p. 6, Table 1; scope in pp. 3–4, Data).
- Distinct student-group exposure patterns: the overall index is −0.32 SD for Hispanic students and −0.19 SD for Black students, versus +0.21 SD for White students; Asian, multiracial, and American Indian/Alaska Native students also have positive overall values (p. 7, Figure 2). These are enrollment-weighted school environments, not measurements of individual classroom exposure.
- The reported fiscal-accounting arithmetic: summing endowment, coefficient, and interaction terms yields approximately 29.9% of the overall gap for property taxes and −17.1% for state building aid (my calculations from pp. 9–10, Table 2; consistent with p. 11, Figure 3). These can be cited as this specification's descriptive allocations, with the incomplete accounting and noncausal interpretation attached.
- A useful extension from spending inputs to observed facility conditions: the article combines item-level and racial-group comparisons with fiscal correlates, while acknowledging prior infrastructure inequality and mixed investment findings (pp. 1–4). This is a defensible contribution without assuming its qualified priority claim has been independently established.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- Claims that changing tax reliance or state aid would eliminate a specified share of the gap: the decomposition combines differences in covariate means and associations and does not estimate funding-policy effects (pp. 4–5; pp. 9–10, Table 2). Property taxes' prominence among plotted factors is not proof that they are the dominant causal mechanism.
- Exact contributor rankings, individual significance markers, and robustness claims: incomplete coefficient accounting and unspecified dependence adjustments limit inference, while expanded-control and alternative-index exhibits are in unavailable online appendices (pp. 9–11, Table 2 and Figure 3; p. 13, note 11). Published component arithmetic can be checked; underlying estimates and robustness have not been independently reproduced.
- Generalizations to every non-White group, all New York schools, present-day conditions, or other states: disaggregated results vary across groups, and the historical inspection sample excludes New York City and does not cover all schools (p. 7, Figure 2; pp. 3–4, Data; p. 13, notes 2–6).
- Claims about achievement, health effects, maintenance quality conditional on facility ownership, or which investments yield the greatest benefit: the study does not estimate student outcomes, validate the composite for those outcomes, or clearly identify denominators for absent facilities (p. 4; p. 6, Table 1; p. 12). These remain questions for other evidence.

#### Verification notes

- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution reviews' main disparities: ventilation 0.768 versus 0.509 and health-office availability 0.930 versus 0.815 appear in Table 1 (p. 6); their differences are −25.9 and −11.5 percentage points (my calculations).
- CONFIRMED — Contribution/writing reviews' group heterogeneity: Figure 2 shows negative overall values for Black and Hispanic students and positive values for the other displayed groups (p. 7); school-composition differences are not identical disadvantages for all non-White groups.
- CONFIRMED — Methods/writing/reproducibility reviews' funding arithmetic: (0.0425 + 0.0151 − 0.0328)/0.0830 = 29.9% for property taxes and (−0.0107 + 0.0118 − 0.0153)/0.0830 = −17.1% for aid (my calculations, pp. 9–10, Table 2), consistent with Figure 3 (p. 11).
- CONFIRMED — Methods/writing reviews' accounting concern: the reported coefficient subtotal “0.0603**” exceeds the displayed coefficient-row sum of −0.0095 by 0.0698 (my calculation, pp. 9–10, Table 2); attributing this to an omitted intercept remains an inference.
- CONFIRMED — Reviews' sample discrepancy: “2,352 unique schools” (p. 4, Data) differs from Table 1's “940,” “912,” and “519” (sum 2,371), and its extreme-group sum 1,459 differs from Table 2's “1,440” observations (my calculations, pp. 6 and 10); a sample transition is plausible but undocumented.
- CONFIRMED — Writing review's transposition: prose gives “Eighty-five percent” for lighting and “75%” for appearance, while Figure 1a gives “Lighting quality good” 0.75 and “Appearance good” 0.85 (p. 5); the figure values govern this guide, without independently validating the underlying data.
- CONFIRMED — Methods review's swimming-pool concern: Table 1 prints “−0.033**” with “**p < .01,” but displayed proportions 0.152 and 0.119 and group sizes 940 and 519 yield an approximate independent-school two-sided p of .074 (my calculation, p. 6, Table 1); the printed marker is unsupported by that stated simple comparison, though raw data are unavailable.
- COULD NOT CHECK — Reported index and expanded-control robustness, detailed coding, and sample-selection comparisons depend on unavailable online appendices (pp. 4, 11, 13); their absence from the supplied PDF does not establish that the authors failed to provide them.

#### Per-Dimension Ratings

| Methods | adequate | high (0.88) |
| Literature | adequate | high (0.85) |
| Writing | weak | high (0.96) |
| Contribution | adequate | high (0.91) |
| Reproducibility | weak | high (0.93) |

## Responses

Authors of the reviewed paper, and readers who find an error in a review, can respond in the discussion thread below (it needs a GitHub account), or open an issue in the site's GitHub repository. Corrections are logged on the Corrections page with dates.
